Title: International Year of the Periodic Table 2019

Part: Periodic Table's unique place (about 150 words)
- Periodic Table holds unique place among scientific accomplishments
- Simple-looking, easily accessible; both reference tool and research tool
- Significance cuts across nearly every discipline; researchers from all sciences keep mining the relationships it organizes
- Lighthouse/beacon of order amid chaos of physical world
- Inspired animation has produced remarkable on-line versions, user friendly to all
- Even set to music

Part: Why 2019 is celebrated (about 130 words)
- 2019 = 150th anniversary of Dmitri Mendeleev's (Russian) discovery of relationships underlying the table
- Also centennial of IUPAC's founding
- IUPAC oversees scientific nomenclature; de facto keeper of the table, keeps it up-to-date and accurate
- UN declared 2019 International Year of the Periodic Table of Chemical Elements (IYPT 2019)
- Celebrates one of the most familiar, powerful scientific accomplishments in human history

Part: Opening ceremony (about 70 words)
- Formal launch at UNESCO offices, Paris
- Presentations on past, present, future of the system
- Lecture by Dutch chemist Ben Feringa, 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry

Part: Diversity events (about 170 words)
- February: two-day symposium on female researchers' contributions to the contemporary table
- Organizers: UNESCO with IUPAC, International Union of the History and Philosophy of Science, European Chemical Society, Real Sociedad Española de Química, University of Murcia
- Global Women's Breakfast, single day, February 12, run by local organizers incl. Canadian events nationwide
- July: World Chemistry Congress and IUPAC General Assembly complete the Periodic Table of Younger Chemists
- Room to add Canadian nominations; so far Kelly Summers (University of Saskatchewan, copper) and Ernest Awoonor-Williams (Memorial University, zinc)

Part: 1001 Inventions initiative (about 60 words)
- British educational organization 1001 Inventions mounting multimedia initiative
- Covers inquiry spanning more than 1200 years, culminating in today's well-organized table

Part: Canadian plans and ElemenTree (about 150 words)
- 102nd Canadian Chemistry Conference and Exhibition (CCCE 2019) celebrates elements and variety of Canadian chemistry
- Conference abstracts grouped by most prominently featured element
- Chemical Institute of Canada (CIC) a big fan of the table; offering members a chance at own copy of a remarkable physical representation
- Called the ElemenTree; developed by late Fernando Dufour, professor at Collège Ahuntsic, Montreal
- CIC offered a number of these keepsakes; watch in 2019 for chance to obtain one, plus more IYPT 2019 announcements

Part: Photo captions (about 30 words)
- Fernando Dufour with several versions of his ElemenTree; photo credit Paul Dufour
- ElemenTree model CIC will make available to some members; photo credit Canada Science and Technology Museum

Title: Rebuilding Local Food in Haliburton

Part: Tourism-Dependent Economy (about 230 words)
- Haliburton, like many Canadian Shield communities: known for wild highlands, countless lakes
- Forestry economy replaced by reliance on tourism
- Locals chide seasonal urbanites, yet urban capital keeps region economically stable
- Same story across much of Ontario, other regions of North America
- Prosperity seems to be waning; least self-reliant communities feel pressure most
- Importing most products means capital must come from outside
- Tourism brings cash but ties fortunes to one industry; like towns abandoned by one big employer
- Works only if tourists exist; more communities turning to tourism, competition for market share heats up
- If status quo lasts, no concern: global economy recovers, tourism dollars keep propping community up
- But what if urban disposable income collapses, tourists stay home?
- Many locals want to be prepared for change; common movement in small towns across continent

Part: Food Energy Manufacturing (about 90 words)
- Cheap food, goods, energy come from far-away jurisdictions, far from most small communities
- Even Southern Ontario, rich farmland, grows mostly corn and soy to feed livestock
- Considerable food imported; manufacturing long gutted
- Energy rests on tenuous international relationships, unwieldy infrastructure
- Community groups formed to fill void should system fail

Part: Haliburton's Food Focus (about 90 words)
- Photo caption: Season Extension, Abbey Gardens
- Haliburton focus: food and agriculture
- If food system disrupted, food scarce at best; already not reaching everyone who needs it
- Rural poverty glaring; access to healthy food inadequate
- Food system reform can prepare for change and address uneven distribution of good food

Part: Lost Self-Reliance (about 180 words)
- Tragedy: past had some self-reliance in food, energy, manufactured goods
- Skills broad and well honed; good land in production; infrastructure to grow and process food in place
- Gaps filled by inter-regional supply lines linking neighbouring communities
- Globalization, in only a couple generations, eroded small-community self-reliance
- Now rely on cheap labour elsewhere, cheap energy to deliver goods
- Depend on corporate imperialism, polluting energy that will eventually doom us
- And for what? Affordable food and goods? Traded self-determination for convenience
- Even with cheap food, many families can't feed themselves well
- Parenthetical: food is a scapegoat; real drain is predatory practices of banks, utilities, insurers, governments, everyone else after your wallet

Part: Growing on the Shield (about 150 words)
- Photo caption: Haliburton Grain CSA Rye
- Vulnerabilities now clear; more people joining food system reform movement
- First challenge: repeated insistence we can't grow food on Canadian Shield
- Won't be capital of corn and soy, or expansive feed lots
- Accumulation of small-scale enterprises could reach critical mass to feed community
- Soil won't withstand cash crop rape; land unsuitable for mechanization; don't repeat past failures
- Agricultural systems exist that grow soil over time; crops thrive in this climate; hope and innovation
- Photo caption: There is a history of farming in Haliburton

Part: Collaboration and Risk (about 180 words)
- Next step after finding mettle: collaborate
- Reform isn't step one to twelve; must happen concurrently, every puzzle piece at once
- Storeowner can't promote local produce without supply
- Farmer can't grow without market
- Bakery can't mill flour from uncleaned grain
- Restaurant can't sell meat not processed in appropriate facility
- Despite supportive organizations, individual entrepreneurs and families take the risk of building new food system; all must co-ordinate and share risk
- Haliburton standing on the edge
- Lacking faith in status quo not enough; watching from comfort zone not an option
- Needed: collective willingness to step forward despite risks

Title: Understanding MOA and Scope Click Values

Part: Intro: MOA in Scopes (about 130 words)
- Most scopes: windage and elevation adjustments referenced to MOA (minute of angle)
- Each click usually 1/4 MOA; some scopes 1/8 MOA
- Shooters call it a fraction of an inch at 100 yards instead of true MOA value
- Inch is easy number; easy to visualize multiples without calculator
- Close enough for practical purposes, esp. up to a few hundred yards; real difference only 0.47 inch at 1000 yards
- For serious target shooting and increasing distances, MOA value vs sight adjustment becomes more essential

Part: Calculating Minute of Angle (about 380 words)
- Arc angle in degrees; 360 degrees in full circle; each degree 60 minutes of arc
- Distance covered by arc relative to circumference (total distance around circle)
- Knowing radius, circumference easily found using pi
- Pi: ratio of circumference to diameter (radius x 2), constant regardless of circle size
- Precise value of pi unknown to man; normally resolved to 3.1416 or 3.141
- Example: circle with 6 inch radius; circumference = (6 x 2) x 3.1416 = 12 x 3.1416 = 37.6992 inches
- 1 degree = 37.6992 / 360 = 0.1047 inch at 6 inches from center
- 1 minute = 0.1047 / 60 = 0.001745 inch at 6 inches
- Knowing MOA lets you calculate its value at any distance
- 6 inches is 1/600th of 100 yards: (100 yards x 36 inches) / 6 inches = 600
- So MOA at 100 yards = 1.047 inches (0.001745 x 600)
- Scaling: 50 yards = 1/2 the 100 yard value; 70% @ 70 yards; twice @ 200 yards; 6 times @ 600 yards; and so on
- Difference between inches vs MOA thinking: 0.47 inch @ 1000 yards
- Four clicks = 1.047 inch change @ 100 yards for 1/4 MOA per click scopes
- Group size in inches: spell out 'inch'; the symbol (") inaccurate and misleading since it also means 'second of angle' (1/60 of a minute of angle)
- Write '1 inch' not 1"
- Could write 1' (symbol for minute of angle) but may mislead those thinking in feet

Part: Why Use MOA (about 230 words)
- Angle value easily calculated to any distance from origin: center of circle or muzzle of barrel
- MOA part of our only universal language, mathematics
- Rifle precision in inches also scalable to other distances, but need both distance and inch measure (e.g. 1 inch @ 100 yards)
- With angle, only the angle measure is needed
- Example: 0.73 inch @ 100 yards vs 0.7 MOA (0.73 / 1.0472 = 0.697)
- Practically equal (1 MOA = 1.047 inch @ 100 yards) but MOA expression more concise, no distance included
- Two sites for further discussion: 'What Is MOA and Is It Really an Inch At 100 Yards?' and 'Mil-dots and Minutes-of-angle, From a Technical Perspective'
- Metric countries: 27.77 mm @ 100 meter used, same proportion as 1 MOA = 1.000 inch @ 100 yard

Part: Calculating Scope Click (about 200 words)
- Long ranges with varying distances: wise to know actual value of each adjustment, esp. if settings changed in field
- Not all scopes precisely calibrated to MOA or to the inch
- Method: shoot from solid bench rest; find group center via Average Group Radius method
- Without reaching scope adjustment limit, make and record as many elevation clicks as keep group on target, same aiming point
- Find center of second group with Average Group Radius method
- Return elevation to previous setting
- Measure distance between the two group centers; divide by number of elevation clicks used for group two = calculated value per click at that distance
- High power rifles: target no less than 100 yards; some projectiles may not stabilize at shorter distances, giving false indication of true performance

Title: 13 Unsolved Mysteries of Earth

Part: Intro (about 44 words)
- Explored planet core to surface; seem ready for space travel
- Earth still surprising us
- Bright Side shares 13 facts about our world with no explanation

Part: 13. Never reached mantle (about 71 words)
- Seismologists: inner core solid, outer core liquid and molten
- Next mantle, crust floating on top
- Mantle composition unknown, never reached
- Mantle depth 30 km to 2,900 km
- Deepest well: Kola borehole, Russia, only 12.3 km

Part: 12. Poles can change (about 37 words)
- Magnetic poles can move, even change direction; happened many times
- Latest switch 10 million years ago; probably will recur
- No one knows why

Part: 11. Two moons (about 46 words)
- Earth had two satellites about 4.6 million years ago, per astronomers
- Second ~1,200 km across, same orbit as Moon, until collision
- Cataclysm may explain why Moon's two sides differ

Part: 10. Moonquakes (about 46 words)
- Few know earthquakes occur on Moon
- Weaker than terrestrial ones, very rare
- Theory: tidal forces of Sun and Earth, plus falling meteorites

Part: 9. Earth spins fast (about 45 words)
- Rotation 1,600 km/h; orbit around Sun 108,000 km/h
- We feel movement only when speed changes
- Constant speed plus gravity: no sensation

Part: 8. Time is growing (about 40 words)
- 620M years ago day was 21.9 hours
- Earth slowing ~70 msec per 100 years
- 100M years needed for 24-hour day

Part: 7. Strange gravity (about 41 words)
- Not a perfect sphere, so high- and low-gravity areas
- Example: Hudson Bay, Canada
- Weak gravity due to low density from rapidly melting glaciers

Part: 6. Hottest and coldest (about 47 words)
- Hottest: Aziziya, Libya, up to +58°С
- Coldest place: Antarctic, down to -73°С
- Lowest observed: Russian Vostok Station, July 21, 1983, -89.2°С

Part: 5. Severe pollution (about 42 words)
- Not really news
- Astronauts say 1978 view of Earth was different
- Space debris and waste turning blue, green, white planet brown, gray, black

Part: 4. Iron, oxygen, silicon (about 47 words)
- Composition: 32.1% iron, 30.1% oxygen, 15.1% silicon, 13.9% magnesium
- ~90% of iron thought to be in core
- Crust holds most oxygen (47%)

Part: 3. Purple Earth (about 31 words)
- Ancient plants used retinal, not chlorophyll, to absorb light
- Reflected red and blue, not green, giving purple
- Some bacteria still use retinal

Part: 2. Hidden ocean (about 67 words)
- Huge water pool deep below surface at 410-660 km
- 2.7 billion years old; found via ringwoodite in mantle
- Water under immense pressure; volume fills Earth's oceans three times
- Theory: oceans appeared from an underground oceanic explosion

Part: 1. Life on Mars (about 70 words)
- After years of speculation, encouraging signs a vital molecule for life is on Mars
- Seen in formations in Gale crater
- Large carbon-based molecules remain in Martian soil, not just rover contamination
- Suggests Mars had life long before Earth

Notes:
Title: Avalanche vs Zener Breakdown in Diodes

Part: Intro: junction and breakdown (about 90 words)
- Basic semiconductor: junction forms from interaction of p-type and n-type
- Junction can be doped heavily or lightly depending on circumstances
- Basic p-n diode conducts in forward bias
- In reverse bias it can't conduct; breakdowns arise
- Causes: carrier multiplication; high doping concentration at junction
- Two types: (1) Avalanche breakdown, (2) Zener breakdown

Part: What is Avalanche Breakdown? (about 230 words)
- Reverse bias: diode non-conducting, yet some movement due to minority carriers
- Current from minority charge = reverse saturation current; responsible for avalanche breakdown
- Junction = interface of p and n material; depletion region exists there
- Both types have majority and minority carriers; in reverse bias focus is minority carriers: electrons in p-type, holes in n-type
- Depletion width variable, depends on bias supplied
- Reverse bias: region wider, affects working; but minority carriers gain enough kinetic velocity to overcome junction barrier
- Collisions occur, generating free charges; process continues, more free carriers = carrier multiplication
- Result: reverse current flows, avalanche breakdown
- Can damage junction completely; non-refundable (irreversible)

Part: What is Zener Breakdown? (about 190 words)
- Junction from p and n interaction; depletion region at junction
- Region width also depends on doping concentration, light or heavy
- Width and doping inversely related: heavy doping = minimum width, and vice versa
- Highly doped junction undergoes zener breakdown
- Minimum width: free charges present tend to cross junction; highest electric field intensity gives rapid carrier movement
- Gives free carriers and reverse current; eliminates depletion region = zener breakdown
- Depletion region returns once reverse voltage removed
- Wrap-up: breakdown types under reverse bias discussed

Part: Avalanche and Zener Diodes (about 110 words)
- Avalanche diode: designed to operate in reverse bias; junction lightly doped; special category
- Symbol same for zener and avalanche diodes
- Basic p-n diode can't operate in reverse bias; special diode needed, normal in forward bias, tolerates reverse currents
- This is the zener diode; good doping concentration at junction

Part: Difference between Zener and Avalanche Breakdown (about 230 words)
- Both occur in reverse bias; zener breakdown voltage comparatively lower than avalanche
- Avalanche cause: collisions between carriers; Zener: high electric field intensity
- Depletion region: avalanche thick; zener thin
- Doping at junction: avalanche minimum; zener high
- Avalanche: pair of electrons and holes produced; zener: mainly electrons
- Electric field: avalanche low; zener strong
- Temperature coefficient: avalanche positive; zener negative
- Ionization: avalanche from collision effect; zener from strong field
- Breakdown voltage and temperature: avalanche directly related; zener inversely
- After breakdown: avalanche voltage tends to vary; zener voltage unaffected
- Avalanche junction destroyed completely, can't recover; zener junction returns to normal when reverse voltage removed

Part: Closing question (about 40 words)
- Analysis of breakdown types done; each has own standards
- Asks which diode, avalanche or zener, is used in protection circuitry

Notes:
Title: Hidden Fees Block Ontario Students' Extracurricular Learning

Part: Hidden costs open (about 50 words)
- Hidden costs are what kill
- Cellphone analogy: hunt for best/cheapest phone, then system-access fee
- Education same: invest to make best/cheapest, then student-activity fees

Part: Barrier to learning (about 100 words)
- Cost of learning outside classroom is staggering
- Some students pay massive fees for sports, drama, art, clubs
- Involvement in school life costs money; being good at a sport brings a financial penalty
- Ontario schools have ingrained barrier to experiential learning
- Systematic barrier directly challenges poverty reduction and equity in education
- Ministry of Education must confront it

Part: Ministry and TDSB action (about 50 words)
- Ministry asking school boards for a 'snapshot' of fees charged to students
- Tomorrow, Toronto District School Board debates motion for standard board-wide fee, first step to control

Part: Why extracurriculars matter (about 120 words)
- Ministry definitions treat extracurriculars as an 'extra', over and above basic education
- But needed to build school community, let students own their education, work of own volition, achieve own goals
- Experiential learning can be difference between engaged and disengaged student
- Children fighting obesity; character education sometimes best taught on football field
- Need more access, not less; ministry must open doors for engaged, healthy, well-behaved students

Part: The fees in numbers (about 140 words)
- Boards need to understand hidden costs
- More than 77 per cent of schools charge some activity fee; prices up more than 50 per cent
- Most high schools charge activity card at start of term; average $35
- This 'start-of-term levy' is first of a long litany of costs
- Study in a provincial-barometer board: one team membership up to $455
- No way to 'buy in bulk'; volleyball plus rugby near $1,000; add student council or drama and cost like university tuition

Part: Perverse message (about 60 words)
- High costs a problem, and the message is detrimental
- Winning a tournament means paying for the next one
- Student penalized for doing well; can discourage excellence in extracurriculars

Part: Boards lack oversight (about 90 words)
- Scary: fees often unknown to boards
- Schools charge club by club, no central authority on amounts
- Study in the average board showed massive range of fees, even between schools a few blocks apart
- Conclusion: boards have no handle on fees students pay to explore talents outside classroom

Part: Equity impact (about 90 words)
- Fees are a major challenge to equity
- Some schools more affordable than others; sports cheaper at one school than another
- Lower-income students face fees limiting participation, worsening trials of fitting in and succeeding
- Truly equitable system, key to poverty reduction, requires removing fees

Part: Recommended steps (about 90 words)
- First: each board finds out how much students are asked to pay
- Then ministry begins funding extracurriculars with non-profits and other ministries, and phases out fees
- Remove barrier to invaluable part of school
- Reach every Ontario student with quality education, including experiential learning

Notes:
Title: Curiosity and Memory

Part: Opening scenario (about 65 words)
- Studying boring facts for next-day exam; give up, watch documentary on fascinating subject
- Afterward can't recall a single exam fact, but remember tiniest documentary details

Part: What's known about memory (about 45 words)
- Easier to learn interesting than boring material, but how curiosity affects memory still mysterious
- Comparatively little known about how memories formed and stored in brain

Part: H.M. case (about 115 words)
- First major insight into human memory: Henry Gustav Molaison (H.M.), one of most studied patients in neuroscience history
- Epilepsy; surgery at age 27 removing brain areas thought to cause it
- Surgery worked for epilepsy but caused severe anterograde amnesia
- Couldn't form new memories; spent next 50 years in a steady present
- Attributed to removal of medial temporal lobes
- Later experiments: hippocampus, structure within region, key role in learning and memory

Part: Long term potentiation (about 65 words)
- Decades of research identified potential memory mechanism: long term potentiation (LTP)
- Two neurons stimulated together multiple times: electrical connection strength increases, better signal transmission
- Strengthened connections thought to underlie new associations and storage of new memories

Part: The curious case of the curious brain: study design (about 105 words)
- Question: how do complex psychological concepts like curiosity fit this picture? Recent study in journal Neuron on curiosity's effect on learning
- Subjects saw series of trivia questions, rated curiosity about each answer
- Brain activity monitored in MRI scanner while selected question shown, then answer
- Before answer, shown picture of neutral face, unrelated to task
- After scan, tested on memory of trivia answers and of faces

Part: Findings (about 130 words)
- Curiosity improved memory for trivia questions and also for faces shown after them
- Curiosity ratings linked to higher activation of nucleus accumbens, substantia nigra, ventral tegmental area
- These areas previously linked to extrinsic reward-related memory: rewards from outside world, like food or money
- Reward here, curiosity satisfied, came from within
- Suggests common mechanism shared between extrinsic and intrinsic reward-related memory
- Authors suggest mechanism may involve dopamine release, neurotransmitter already linked to learning and extrinsic reward

Part: Implications (about 65 words)
- Can we harness curiosity to help learning?
- Possibly drugs acting on dopaminergic system could one day boost learning and memory, acting on same circuits as interesting-material learning
- For now, message for educators

Notes:
Title: 4D Medicine's biodegradable polymer inks for 3D-printed biomedical uses

Part: 3D printing in medicine (about 150 words)
- 3D printing developed 1980s; many medical uses since
- Helps surgeons: patient-specific organ replicas to practise on before complicated operations
- Also provides surgical tools, custom-made prosthetics
- Potential to ease organ transplantation limits: personalised tissue engineering scaffolds, in situ tissue defect repair with cells, directly printed implants
- Univ. of Birmingham, UK researchers developed biodegradable polymer inks to take tech a step further

Part: The resin inks (about 190 words)
- Resin inks based on aliphatic polycarbonates
- Unlike other polycarbonates, no aromatic groups between carbonate linkages, so less rigid
- Founder Andrew Dove uses thiol-ene click chemistry to crosslink cyclic carbonate monomers; makes 3D polycarbonate structures that print flexibly
- Dove: big step is precise design of monomer and monomer mixture
- Multiple carbonate monomers give resins with different cured mechanical properties, e.g. tuned to specific degradation rate
- Dove: properties tunable, big advantage; control microstructure, macroscopic shape, everything; unusual

Part: Applications and safety (about 270 words)
- Range of potential applications; first aim: devices filling tissue void after intrusive surgery
- Example: breast cancer removal surgery; recovery a big problem, hard to reconstruct tissue, takes several operations
- Resins printed into unique support structure for tissue regrowth after tumour removal
- Scaffolds fill tumour void, help direct radiotherapy, improving outcomes and survival rates
- Scaffold degrades, leaving only natural tissue
- Dove: any shape and size; data show no real reaction when implanted
- Thiol-ene chemistry avoids potentially toxic residual acrylate groups other biomaterial scaffolds rely on
- Four month rat study done; further animal studies under way, shorter and longer implant periods, to see response across lifecycle
- Paediatric uses too, e.g. musculoskeletal problems; bespoke printed products in different sizes fit growing child's body
- Dove: designing devices, studying performance, feel, what patients want

Part: Down to business (about 210 words)
- Dove and business partner Andrew Weems spun out 4D Medicine from the University to move technology toward market approval
- Weems instrumental in development; as PhD student contacted Dove about linking their 3D printing and shape memory experience, seeing biomedical interest
- Weems won Whitaker International Program fellowship to work with Dove; fast progress, opportunity to do something impactful
- Weems later got Innovate UK Innovation and Commercialisation of University Research (Icure) funding, financing researchers to explore commercial potential
- Both funding rounds essential; Dove: funding always biggest hurdle; Whitaker fellowship a turning point as hard to get funding for such an idea
- Pair won Royal Society of Chemistry Emerging Technologies competition, 2018

Part: Regulatory road ahead (about 100 words)
- Dove and Weems seeking investment for final steps to toxicology data proving safety to regulators
- Dove: regulatory hurdles for medical devices big; much work left proving material safety, many steps to approval
- Dove: target application plus material should mitigate risk; initial results point right way; looking really good

Part: Company facts (about 20 words)
- Location: Birmingham, UK
- Employees: 2
- Origin: spin-out from University of Birmingham

Notes:
Title: Preventing and Managing Dairy Pneumonia

Part: Rise in pneumonia cases (about 65 words)
- Penn Vet New Bolton Center (NBC) dairy health experts seeing more pneumonia this year
- Mostly growing heifers and calves
- Cause: wide temperature swings, wet-warm weather in Northeast and Mid-Atlantic
- NBC offers tips for area producers on preventing and managing pneumonia in dairy cows

Part: Ventilation (about 70 words)
- Good ventilation affects air quality and cooling capacity needed to prevent illness
- Keep curtains and windows open for air flow
- Older farms: consider forced or tube installation system in barns
- All operations: benefit from air-quality and air-flow test

Part: Vaccination (about 85 words)
- Key to prevention, only if used correctly
- Consult veterinarian or have them develop operation-specific plan
- Consider adding pneumonia-specific vaccines just before hardest times: early and late winter
- Some intranasal vaccines especially helpful, better localized immunity in airways

Part: Minimizing stress (about 45 words)
- Avoid or minimize extra stressors in winter
- Keep transporting animals, excessive intermingling, bringing in new stock from outside sources or sale barns to a minimum if possible

Part: Monitoring (about 50 words)
- Check animals regularly for signs of illness
- Take temperatures of any showing symptoms
- Early recognition gives best chance of effective treatment and prevents long-term damage

Part: Outbreak response (about 55 words)
- If outbreak occurs, fast aggressive treatment is key
- Treat affected animals early; consider isolating them to limit spread
- Blanket treatments, including feed-through antibiotics, can work for larger outbreaks
- Consult veterinarian first

Notes:
Title: Keeping Stress in Check During COVID-19

Part: Introduction (about 110 words)
- COVID-19 pandemic hard to live through; generational crisis, struck like night-time thief, upended life
- Governments grapple with reviving economy, reshaping acceptable social interactions
- Another battle fought by each of us individually, alone
- We forget mental health also ravaged, undernourished, starving for relief
- Stress meters long in red; prognosis bleak for certain demographics

Part: People Who Are More Prone to Stress (about 170 words)
- Everyone responds to stress differently; some handle earth-shaking changes, others fret over minutiae
- Regardless of tolerance, pandemic especially bad for following groups per CDC
- Higher risk for severe illness (older people, any age with underlying conditions)
- Children and teens
- People caring for family or loved ones
- Frontline workers: health care providers, first responders
- Essential workers in food industry
- Existing mental health conditions
- Substance users or those with substance use disorder
- Lost jobs, reduced hours, other major employment changes
- Disabilities or developmental delay
- Socially isolated: living alone, rural or frontier areas
- Some racial and ethnic minority groups
- No access to information in primary language
- Experiencing homelessness
- Living in congregate (group) settings

Part: Understand the Science Behind Stress (about 120 words)
- Tip 1 of 5 to keep stress in check
- Scene: 200,000 years ago, ancestors resting by watering hole after hunt, laughing; rustle in bush, tiger in dark; hearts pound, sweat beads
- In danger: quickened pulse and breathing, muscle tension = heightened alertness, brain activity; by design to put body in gear for precarious situations
- Same thing today; stress is normal body response; can manage it and even use it to advantage

Part: Dial Down Media Consumption (about 120 words)
- Tip 2: in uncertain times world craves information
- Knowledge tempers anxiety about virus; knowing precautions makes us feel safer
- But easy to get overloaded in 24-hour news cycle
- First, make sure information is reliable; internet can be muddle of semi-truthful muck
- Second, limit daily mainstream news; leans on sensationalism; depressing news we can't control affects us

Part: Do Something You've Always Wanted (about 120 words)
- Tip 3: Atticus poem line
- May be mere locution but profound today
- Everyone home; so much free time; anxious when we realize we're wasting it
- Productivity gets minds off virus
- Perfect time to start first chapter of book or crystallize long-contemplated business plan
- Do something future self will be proud of when all is done

Part: Help Others (about 80 words)
- Tip 4: giving is powerful neural pathway to happiness
- Brain hardwired to release oxytocin, serotonin, dopamine, the trifecta of happiness, in response to altruism
- Money helps, but can also give time, talents, expertise; no shortage of people who'd appreciate it now

Part: Take Care of Yourself (about 110 words)
- Tip 5: mental well-being and physical health two sides of same coin, body and mind; monitor physical condition
- Pandemic left routines in shambles; exercise less, binge-watch Netflix, eat embarrassing amounts of junk food; ugly side of staying home
- Refuse to let virus hijack parts of life we can control
- New normal is hard but shouldn't be hopeless
